title: Is this farewell to MFN, the non-discrimination principle of the world trading system?
date_evidence: Is this farewell to MFN, the non-discrimination principle of the world trading system? ... publication date of March 2, 2026
key_claim: The most-favoured-nation (MFN) principle of non-discrimination, which broadly characterised world trade in the 21st century (more than 80% of world merchandise trade in 2022 took place under MFN terms), is being abandoned. Because of exceptional above-floor tariffs, only about 10% (10.3%) of US merchandise imports now enter under MFN terms, versus around 40% (42.4%) for China and more than 75% (79.0%) for the European Union. In January 2026, EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic proposed to weaken European observance of unconditional MFN, tying low tariffs to 'fair' practices; the US and EU, which wrote MFN into GATT Article I, are now departing from it.
frame_summary: PIIE argues that the US, and now potentially the EU, is abandoning the WTO's founding non-discrimination principle, a shift that would damage the global economy if it spreads.
notes: Structural anchor (02/03/2026): the canonical analytical spine for the MFN-abandonment core of the signal. Import-share figures from the article's Table 1 (US 10.3%, China 42.4%, EU 79.0%, 2025). Publication date confirmed via WebSearch; article references the 20 February 2026 Supreme Court ruling and the January 2026 Sefcovic proposal, consistent with a 2 March 2026 date. Authors Gary Clyde Hufbauer and Ye Zhang.

title: US reciprocal trade deals built to push America's trade partners away from China
key_claim: As of 22 May 2026, nine Agreements on Reciprocal Trade (ARTs) had been signed (Argentina, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Indonesia, Malaysia and Taiwan), with more under negotiation. The deals go far beyond tariffs: they use seven recurring legal mechanisms (forced-labour exclusions, coordinated third-country restrictions, third-country-controlled-firm provisions, export-control alignment, investment screening, rules of origin, and penalty clauses) to pull partners away from China and require them to keep US market access on conditions set by Washington. The ARTs mark the first large-scale use of US tariffs to enforce alignment with American policy choices since the end of the Cold War, and represent a departure from WTO constraints on discriminatory tariff rates. Their enforcement base is legally shaky: the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA 'Liberation Day' tariffs and a replacement balance-of-payments tariff was struck down by the Court of International Trade, so USTR is leaning on new Section 301 investigations.
frame_summary: PIIE argues the Agreements on Reciprocal Trade are a discriminatory architecture that conditions US market access on partners' alignment against China, replacing rules-based trade with negotiated conditions.
notes: In-window (04/06/2026), authors Mary E. Lovely and Christine Y. Wan. Also supplies the China US-import-share shift (22% before the 2018-19 war to 9% by end-2025) and the enforcement-fragility point (SCOTUS and CIT rulings; Section 301 initiations of March 2026).

title: EU-US trade: Parliament gives its green light to tariff legislation
key_claim: MEPs gave final approval to two regulations implementing the EU's tariff commitments under the August 2025 EU-US joint statement reached at Turnberry on 27 July 2025. The main regulation, adopted by 440 votes to 151 with 50 abstentions, eliminates tariffs on all US industrial goods and grants preferential access for US seafood and agri-food goods; tariff preferences expire on 31 December 2029 unless renewed (a sunset clause). Parliament added a suspension clause, a safeguard mechanism and quarterly reporting, so the Commission can suspend preferences if the US fails to uphold the deal or imposes above-15% tariffs on EU steel and aluminium derivatives.
frame_summary: The European Parliament frames the legislation as converting the EU's joint-statement commitments into binding law while arming the EU with a defensive toolbox against US non-compliance.
notes: In-window (plenary vote 15/06/2026; press release ref 20260611IPR45206, meta plenaryDate 15-06-2026). Shows the managed, asymmetric character of the EU-US deal: the EU eliminates all industrial tariffs while the US holds a 15% ceiling, with the deal locked into EU law and hedged by suspension clauses.

title: EU-US trade: Council gives final approval for the tariff commitments under Joint Statement
date_evidence: On June 25, 2026, the Council of the European Union adopted two Regulations implementing the EU's tariff commitments under the Joint Statement
key_claim: On 25 June 2026 the Council of the European Union gave final approval to two Regulations implementing the EU's tariff commitments under the 21 August 2025 EU-US Joint Statement; the EU eliminated all duties on US industrial goods and improved access for certain non-sensitive agri-food products from 1 July 2026, while the US side replaces the 10% Section 122 tariff with a 15% all-inclusive ceiling on most EU goods.
frame_summary: The Council frames its approval as stabilising transatlantic trade by turning the EU's political commitments into binding law.
notes: In-window (25/06/2026). The consilium.europa.eu press page renders its body via JavaScript (empty on WebFetch); the date and substance are corroborated by the Sullivan & Cromwell memo (29/06/2026), which cites the same 25 June 2026 Council adoption, and by the European Parliament release. Date encoded in the press-release URL path (2026/06/25).

title: America First investment pledges: Big numbers but uncertain results
key_claim: The Trump administration's America First Investment Policy has extracted more than $5 trillion in investment commitments from partners including Japan ($550 billion), Saudi Arabia (nearly $1 trillion), the EU, the Gulf states, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan. The pledges are 'clouded with uncertainty': most lack a clear framework for monitoring and verification, most fall short of binding treaties, and for several Gulf states the commitments (nearly $4 trillion) strain credibility. PIIE characterises the deals as a transactional, extractive, pay-for-protection approach, negotiated under the threat of tariffs, that outsources US industrial-policy financing to allies and circumvents Congress.
frame_summary: PIIE argues the headline investment pledges are large but structurally uncertain and coercive, unlikely to materialise as advertised.
notes: Structural-context source in the 3-6m band (27/01/2026, not flagged as the single structural anchor), authors Gregory Auclair and Adnan Mazarei. Supplies the quantitative-pledge scale and the enforceability/instability core of the signal; the pledge structures (July 2025 Japan, November 2025 Saudi) remain the current terms.

title: EU Implements Tariff Commitments Under the EU-U.S. Trade Deal
key_claim: The EU's two Implementing Regulations (adopted by the Council on 25 June 2026) totally eliminate customs duties on most US industrial goods and open 20 duty-free or reduced-duty tariff-rate quotas for US agricultural and seafood products, while retaining a fixed 'entry price' floor on 15 categories of fresh produce. The Regulations 'convert political commitments into binding EU law' and include safeguard and suspension mechanisms letting the Commission suspend the preferences if the US fails to implement or undermines the Joint Statement or discriminates against EU operators. Businesses are advised to verify US-origin eligibility, monitor quota volumes, and address suspension risk in pricing, sourcing and tariff pass-through provisions in contracts.
frame_summary: Sullivan & Cromwell frames the new EU Regulations as binding but conditional and reversible, advising businesses to manage the resulting compliance and suspension risks.
notes: In-window (29/06/2026). Corroborates the Council's 25 June adoption and supplies the concrete managed-trade mechanics: 20 quotas, retained price floors, asymmetric 0%-vs-15% treatment, and the suspension clause. Practitioner (law-firm) source used as directional corroboration and for business-facing implications.

title: Tracking Trump's Trade Deals
key_claim: CFR's tracker of the Trump administration's framework trade deals notes that 'the president has set out to rewrite the rules of trade, one deal at a time', with deals combining tariff terms, purchase commitments and large investment pledges (for example Japan's $550 billion investment pledge). The most novel aspect is the deals' strong focus on 'economic security', covering commitments to mirror US trade actions toward third countries, establish investment screening, exclude certain countries from procurement, and cooperate on supply-chain resilience. On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs, while Section 232 and Section 301 tariffs remain in place.
frame_summary: CFR frames the deals as a case-by-case rewrite of trade rules centred on economic-security conditions rather than reciprocal tariff liberalisation.
notes: Living tracker with a stated 'Published March 17, 2026' date (3-6m band, not flagged as the single structural anchor). Supplies the 'economic security' framing of the deals and the SCOTUS/Section 232-301 enforcement backdrop.
